As of 425 AM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Scattered showers and storms are expected today into 
tonight. Storms may be strong to severe with damaging wind gusts, 
locally heavy rainfall, and isolated large hail possible.

Aloft, the ridge remains in place across the central CONUS with a 
trough across coastal New England gradually pushing west towards the 
local area today. This will allow for the amplified belt of NW/NNW 
flow aloft to remain centered from Ohio into VA and NC. Similar to 
yesterday, this will place a large portion of the local area under a 
favorable corridor for storms. At the surface, a cold front was 
located north of the local area and will gradually move south 
through the day. The most notable change from yesterday has 
been that the FROPA looks to be slower. WPC places the cold 
front from central VA into SE VA this afternoon with the front 
lingering across a portion of the local area into the evening 
before eventually moving south into NC. Given the slower FROPA, 
the warm sector will likely remain across at least the SW half 
of the area and could extend even farther NE. The 00z CAMs were 
in general agreement that storms currently across the southern 
Great Lakes into Ohio will become an MCS and follow the NW flow 
aloft towards the Appalachians by late morning. There are two 
main scenarios afterwards. The first possibility is that the MCS
holds together as it crosses the mountains and restrengthens 
east of the mountains as a line of storms with straight-line 
winds moving across the local area. The second option is that 
the MCS breaks apart once it reaches the mountains and the 
remnant vorticity helps a combination of supercells and 
multicells form across the local area this afternoon. These 
storms would be capable of both damaging winds and large hail. 
In either case, confidence has increased in severe storms today 
across much of the area. The most likely timeframe for severe 
weather looks to be 2-10 PM. However, some CAMs have convection
as early as 10 AM with others showing some severe potential 
lingering into the evening. The severe potential tapers off 
overnight, however, scattered showers or storms will continue to
be possible through the night across southern portions of the 
area.

Environmentally, HREF shows CAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg across the 
area with lower values across the Northern Neck and Eastern 
Shore. Meanwhile, shear of 35-45 kt overlaps the instability, 
creating a favorable balance for severe weather. Additionally, 
the general model consensus is for mid-level lapse rates of 
6-6.5C this afternoon which adds confidence in severe weather. 
Given the increasingly favorable parameters for severe weather, 
SPC has expanded the slight risk (level 2/5) to now include the 
I-64 corridor and locations south. The marginal (level 1/5) risk
has also been expanded and now includes the Northern Neck and 
Virginia Eastern Shore. Damaging winds are the primary hazard, 
however, given the favorable shear and mid-level lapse rates, 
large hail will also be possible if supercells are realized (as 
opposed to line segments). In fact, if a discrete supercell were
to form, hail larger than 1 inch in diameter (potentially up to
ping ball sized) isn't out of the question. The best chance for
this is if a supercell is able to latch onto the cold front 
since the front could be oriented NW to SE which follows the NW 
flow aloft. Additionally, while tornadoes are unlikely given 
weak 0-1 km SRH, a tornado cannot be ruled out if a supercell is
able to interact with the cold front given lower LCLs. Will 
note that the limiting factors for today's severe threat are the
potential for lingering stability (CIN) from yesterday's 
convection and northerly surface winds. However, given a lack of
cloud cover this morning, destabilization (and the erosion of 
any lingering CIN) appears likely.

Severe weather will not be the only potential hazard. WPC has also 
expanded the slight risk for excessive rainfall (ERO) today to 
include the I-64 corridor and locations to the south given the 
potential for heavy rain and localized flooding. Given the shear in 
place, individual showers/storms should be moving (as opposed to 
being stationary) which should help limit the flooding potential 
outside of training. However, heavy rain rates within storms and 
localized training of storms could allow for localized flooding, 
mainly across urban areas. Shower/storm chances decrease Sun (15-40% 
PoPs) with most convection likely confined to the far southern 
portions of the area (or remaining south altogether). Beyond Sun, 
dry conditions are expected early next week, potentially continuing 
into midweek.

with a brief warmup by midweek.
